tier_reason: The independent lzbench 2.4 README table (public harness inikep/lzbench, tag v2.4; release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 built with gcc 15.2.0; single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar, -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4) lists lzo1x 2.10 -1 at 500 / 561 MB/s, 47.45% next to zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%. The v2.4 Makefile builds both lz/lzo (LZO_FILES rule, line 1364) and lz/zlib (ZLIB_FILES rule, line 1400) with CFLAGS = -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing -ffast-math -O3 -DNDEBUG under gcc, so code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all public, consistent with the retier-02 A verdicts for FastLZ, BriefLZ and memlz on the same table.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 49 stars, 44 forks on the unofficial nemequ/lzo GitHub mirror (11 commits, one per release 2.00 to 2.10); LZO ships as liblzo2 in many Linux distributions, the Linux kernel carries its own LZO1X port, and lzbench bundles lzo 2.10
corrections.caveats: Tier A rests on the lzbench 2.4 README run (public Makefile, gcc 15.2.0, EPYC 9555P), where lzbench builds LZO 2.10 and zlib 1.3.2 itself with the same -O3 -ffast-math flags. The win is over stock zlib only: on the same table LZ4 1.10.0 (550 / 3832 MB/s at 47.60%) compresses slightly faster at a similar ratio and decompresses about 6.8x faster, Snappy 1.3.1 (457 / 976 MB/s, 47.85%) decompresses faster, zstd 1.5.7 -1 (411 / 1351 MB/s, 34.53%) is close on compression speed with a much smaller output, and libdeflate 1.26 -1 (202 / 783 MB/s, 34.68%) produces deflate-compatible output that decompresses about 1.4x faster than lzo1x -1 (derived from page data); zlib-ng 2.3.3 -1 runs at 196 / 466 MB/s, 44.41%. lzo1x -1 output is about 30% larger than zlib -1 (100,572,537 vs 77,259,029 bytes). The first-party figure ('about 4-5 times faster than the fastest zlib compression level') is prose in doc/LZO.TXT next to a Calgary Corpus table from a Pentium 133 that has no zlib row. License is GPL-2.0-or-later (source headers: 'either version 2 of the License, or (at your option) any later version'), so linking it into non-GPL software needs a separate commercial license, which doc/LZO.TXT says the author offers. The canonical site http://www.oberhumer.com/opensource/lzo was not opened (egress block); repo, license and release data come from the unofficial nemequ/lzo mirror, whose last commit is the 2.10 release (2017-03-01); lzbench 2.4 also bundles 2.10 dated 2017-03-01.

notes: All quoted numbers match the lzbench 2.4 README rows for lzo1x 2.10 -1 and zlib 1.3.2 -1; the 5.6x compression and 1.9x decompression ratios are correctly marked as derived. The compile flags in the record (including -ffast-math) match the v2.4 Makefile for a gcc build. Shortcomings to record: only beats stock zlib (LZ4, Snappy, zstd -1 and libdeflate -1 match or beat it on the same table), 30% larger output than zlib -1, GPL-2.0-or-later copyleft, unofficial mirror with no release since 2017. Not a duplicate of any listed entry.
